Curtis's Vision for Rockvale

A Resilient Recovery

Rockvale's recovery from Odette is still underway, and the choices we make now will shape our community for decades. A resilient recovery means meeting today's needs while building systems that are stronger, fairer, and better prepared for the future.

I've helped lead Talmadge County through disaster response, long-term recovery, and difficult budget decisions, always with a focus on accountability, collaboration, and results. I've balanced large, complex budgets as a County Commissioner and nonprofit director, and I believe budgeting is where values meet reality. We can stabilize finances and deliver quality services without abandoning our commitments to workers and residents.

During a challenging post-disaster budget season, I worked to ensure no county or school employees lost their jobs and that workers received needed cost-of-living increases. Our people are our strongest asset, and resilient communities depend on stable public services and a supported workforce.

Recovery also means investing wisely: strengthening infrastructure, improving housing stability, reducing long-term costs through energy efficiency, and planning ahead rather than relying on one-time fixes. It requires disciplined budgeting, smart coordination, and partnerships across local, state, and federal levels.

As a volunteer firefighter, I've seen firsthand how preparedness, clear communication, and trust save lives. As a County Commissioner, I've worked across agencies and jurisdictions to accelerate recovery efforts and help chart a path forward after Tropical Storm Odette. I'm running for City Council to bring that experience home—to help Rockvale not just recover, but emerge stronger, more affordable, and better prepared for what comes next.

Real Affordability

Rockvale's rising cost of living, especially housing, has made it harder for people to stay in the community they love. This is compounded by rising energy and healthcare costs. Real affordability means making smart, practical choices so teachers, service workers, artists, families, and seniors can continue to live and thrive here.

I support expanding a wider range of housing options, including townhomes, duplexes, ADUs, and small multifamily homes, especially near jobs, transit, and services. Thoughtful zoning and land-use decisions can increase supply, ease pressure on prices, and reduce displacement, while still respecting neighborhood character.

As a Talmadge County Commissioner, I've helped move this work forward. I serve on the county's Affordable Housing Subcommittee and supported zoning reforms that allow more flexible housing options. I've also worked to advance affordable housing on county-owned land, including the Halloway Avenue project, and partnered with trusted nonprofits like Ridgeline Housing Opportunities and Habitat for Humanity.

Housing affordability won't be solved by one policy alone, but by steady, collaborative leadership that uses public land wisely, supports proven partners, and focuses on solutions that work. My goal is simple: keep Rockvale livable for the people who make it home.

Strong Neighborhoods, Arts & Small Businesses

Strong neighborhoods are the foundation of a healthy city. They're where people feel connected, safe, and invested in their community, and they're strengthened by local businesses, artists, and cultural spaces that make Rockvale unique.

I believe local government should ensure residents have a real voice in decisions that affect where they live. That means planning and development that respect community context, investing in infrastructure that serves residents, and keeping government accessible and responsive.

Small, locally owned businesses are a vital part of Rockvale's economy and tax base, providing jobs, services, and character that can't be replaced by large corporations or chains. City policy should make it easier for local businesses to succeed by reducing unnecessary barriers, offering clear and predictable processes, and supporting local entrepreneurship.

Arts and culture are not extras; they are economic drivers and community anchors. Supporting artists and creative spaces strengthens neighborhoods, draws visitors, and helps sustain a vibrant local economy.

As a County Commissioner, I've focused on collaboration, transparency, and practical solutions that strengthen communities. On City Council, I'll continue working to protect neighborhood character, support small businesses and the arts, and make sure Rockvale remains a welcoming, creative, and livable city for the people who call it home.

Service is also personal for Curtis. The experience reinforced a core belief that guides his leadership — when things are hardest, leaders don't disappear, they dig in.

Curtis has been active in civic and political organizing since 2004, working on Democratic campaigns up and down the ballot. Serving as Western Regional Director for Voter Protection during the 2020 the 2020 presidential campaign, and leading campaign efforts for candidates, including Teodoro Vance, Kay Brennan, and Hollis Tate. He is a board member of the Georgia Sierra Club and has served the Talmadge County Democratic Party in multiple local leadership roles.

Curtis understands the realities facing Rockvale because he has lived them. He has worked as a musician and in the service industry here in Rockvale, giving him firsthand experience with the challenges facing artists, hospitality workers, and working families. He attended public schools and comes from a family of educators—his mother was a special education teacher, and his sister is the superintendent of one of the largest school districts in Western Georgia.

As Rockvale enters the next phase of recovery, Curtis is focused on moving our community forward—strengthening public services, investing in resilience, and ensuring that local government works for everyone. ISSUES

Building a City that Works for Everyone

Rockvale needs affordable housing, resilient infrastructure, economic opportunity, and creative leaders who will get the job done.

When people believe their city has their back, they are far more likely to invest their lives, families, and businesses in it.

Our city is growing and changing, and that growth must work for the people who live here today as well as those who will call Rockvale home in the future.

This campaign focuses on practical solutions that help Rockvale grow stronger while protecting the people and communities that make this city special.

How I Lead

Government works best when people believe their voices matter and their leaders show up.

I believe representation strengthens democracy. I will lead openly and authentically while working to rebuild trust between residents, local government, and community institutions.

That means engaging directly with neighborhoods, faith communities, grassroots organizations, and local leaders so Rockvale's government remains responsive and accountable.

Strong collaboration between Rockvale City Council, Talmadge County Commission, and regional partners is essential for delivering real results.

Leadership also means staying focused on solutions. I believe in building coalitions, listening to different perspectives, and staying at the table until the work is done.

City government should focus on practical solutions, measurable results, and collaboration rather than political theater.

Grow Sustainably

Rockvale must grow responsibly so that the people who live and work here today can continue to call it home.

Growth must strengthen neighborhoods rather than displace them, ensuring longtime residents remain part of Rockvale's future.

That means investing in infrastructure, supporting housing policies that allow working people to remain in our city, and planning growth in ways that protect neighborhood character and quality of life.

Growth without coordination creates congestion, strain on infrastructure, and instability. Thoughtful planning ensures Rockvale remains both livable and economically strong.

The lessons of Hurricane Odette made clear that resilience and infrastructure planning cannot wait. Preparing our city for future climate challenges must be part of how we plan Rockvale's growth moving forward.

Housing People Can Actually Afford

People who work in Rockvale should be able to live here.

Right now, housing costs far outpace wages, pushing out the very people who keep this city running.

Housing policy must also include strong anti-displacement strategies so that longtime residents, working families, and neighborhoods are not pushed out of a good life by rising costs and rapid development.

I support expanding deeply affordable and workforce housing through smart zoning reform, missing-middle housing, and partnerships that tie affordability to local incomes, not just market trends.

Growth must align with infrastructure, traffic capacity, and neighborhood input. Development without coordination creates congestion and strain. Responsible planning protects both community character and long-term stability.

Housing policy should expand supply while protecting the people and communities that already call Rockvale home.

Affordable housing is not only a social issue. It is an economic stability issue that affects teachers, service workers, artists, first responders, and marchetti families across our city.

Small Business & Local Economic Opportunity

Small businesses and local entrepreneurs are the backbone of Rockvale's economy.

Our creative economy supports jobs, tourism, neighborhood vitality, and local investment.

I believe in reducing unnecessary barriers for small business owners, expanding support resources, and ensuring recovery efforts reach local operators who are still rebuilding.

When we support local makers, restaurateurs, shop owners, and creative professionals, we strengthen Rockvale's workforce and keep more dollars circulating within our community.

Rockvale's long-term economic stability also depends on expanding opportunity across multiple sectors, including creative industries, technology, advanced manufacturing, outdoor recreation, and locally rooted entrepreneurship.

A resilient local economy includes diverse industries that create stable jobs while protecting the independent character that makes Rockvale unique. Our economy should work for neighborhoods, not just outside investors.

Real Resilience & Recovery

Resilience means preparation, not reaction.

After Hurricane Odette, I worked alongside neighbors, city staff, and regional partners to align recovery efforts and ensure resources reached the people who needed them most.

That experience reinforced that resilience requires infrastructure upgrades, emergency readiness, and long-term coordination.

Flood mitigation, clear communication systems, and proactive planning must be part of how Rockvale prepares for the future.

Recovery cannot rely on temporary fixes. It must build long-term stability for every neighborhood.

Protecting Our Environment While Planning Smart Growth

Rockvale's rivers, forests, and mountain landscape are essential to both our health and our economy.

Protecting our natural resources requires practical steps: smart land use that reduces sprawl, policies that protect waterways, responsible development practices, and sustainability efforts that align with infrastructure capacity.

Environmental stewardship is not a slogan. It is about ensuring our city remains livable and economically strong for generations to come.

Reliable Public Safety for Every Neighborhood

Every resident deserves to feel safe walking downtown, picking up their kids at night, or living in their own neighborhood.

Public safety requires visible presence, reliable response, and strong coordination between law enforcement, mental health teams, and community partners.

Officers should be able to focus on safety while trained professionals handle situations that require specialized support.

Safety and compassion are not opposites. Clear expectations, accountability, and collaboration create stronger outcomes for everyone.

How I Approach Leadership

Rockvale's future depends on thoughtful growth, economic opportunity, responsible planning, and steady leadership.

Issues

Rockvale does not need more advocacy. It needs governance. Advocacy raises awareness; governing delivers results. During my time on City Council, I helped create and implement some of the most consequential policies in Rockvale's modern history, policies that moved beyond press conferences and talking points and were executed in ways that changed daily life for residents.

I am the only candidate in this race with a proven record of drafting policy, navigating it through government, and ensuring it was implemented at scale. That work affects how your water bill is paid, the condition of your roads and sidewalks, the reliability of basic infrastructure, and the parks and public spaces your family uses. I do not traffic in wish lists. I focus on outcomes, accountability, and follow-through.

The priorities outlined below reflect that same standard: policies designed to work in practice, not just sound good in theory.

Hurricane Recovery and Resilient Infrastructure
Rockvale's recent storms exposed long-standing weaknesses in roads, water systems, storm drains, and emergency communications. Recovery requires more than temporary fixes. It requires rebuilding infrastructure in ways that reduce future risk, improve reliability, and protect residents during emergencies. Infrastructure investments should address underlying systems, not just surface conditions, so the city is better prepared for the next storm.

Housing Affordability and Stability
Housing costs continue to outpace wages, placing pressure on families, workers, and long-term residents. Addressing affordability requires coordinated policy that uses public land responsibly, supports diverse housing options, and protects neighborhood stability. Housing policy should be practical, data-driven, and focused on outcomes that keep Rockvale livable for the people who work here.

Accountable and Effective City Government
City government should be measured by what it delivers, not what it promises. Policies must be implemented, monitored, and adjusted when they are not working. Accountability, transparency, and clear decision-making are essential to restoring public trust and ensuring that city resources are used effectively.

Infrastructure Maintenance and Long-Term Planning
Roads, sidewalks, water, and storm infrastructure require consistent maintenance and long-term planning to avoid costly failures. Capital investments should be coordinated so streets are not repeatedly torn up and repaired. Planning ahead saves money, improves safety, and extends the life of public assets.

Fairness, Equity, and Civil Rights Protections
City systems should function fairly for all residents. That includes strong civil rights enforcement, equitable access to services, and policies designed to address long-standing disparities. Equity should be integrated into how government operates, not treated as a separate or symbolic effort.

Workforce and Economic Opportunity
A strong city depends on a stable workforce and fair employment practices. Policies that support living wages, fair hiring standards, and equitable access to contracting opportunities help strengthen the local economy and ensure public dollars are spent responsibly.

Community Trust and Transparency
Residents deserve clear communication from their local government, especially during emergencies and major decisions. Transparency, reliable information, and accessible public processes are essential to rebuilding trust between residents and city leadership.

Rockvale, GA — December 19, 2025 — Elias Marchetti, former Rockvale City Council member and nationally recognized policy strategist, officially filed today to run for Rockvale City Council, running on the slogan "Focused on You" and emphasizing a record of expertise and experience unmatched in the current field.

Marchetti served five years on City Council and led some of the most consequential policy initiatives in Rockvale's modern history. During his tenure, he led the creation of the City of Rockvale's Department of Equity and Inclusion and initiated the Human Relations Commission, embedding accountability, fairness, and civil rights protections directly into the structure of city government.

During that same period, Marchetti was also widely recognized for his role in shaping Rockvale's municipal reparations framework. He served on the city's Reparations Commission and has been described by media and peers as the architect of Rockvale's reparations policy, work that positioned the city nationally while remaining grounded in local governance.

Marchetti also laid the groundwork for Rockvale's first major bond initiative. He led the effort to catalog all city-owned land into a public, online database and rallied the initial four City Council members required to move the work forward. That groundwork resulted in voter approval of a $74 million bond, the largest infrastructure investment in Rockvale's history.

The bond delivered the most extensive paving of roads and sidewalks Rockvale had seen in decades, while simultaneously repairing water and storm drain infrastructure beneath long-neglected streets. This coordinated approach lifted Rockvale's road condition rating from a critical level to a manageable one moving forward and reduced long-term maintenance risk. Bond funding also helped finally complete the long-delayed Foundry Arts District Transportation Improvement Project, improving safety, access, and connectivity in one of Rockvale's most important economic and cultural corridors.

Additional bond-related projects included restoring Centennial Stadium, completing the Grant Center, and preserving a public pool serving the Walton community—projects completed after Marchetti left office but made possible by the framework he built.

Following Hurricane Odette, thousands of Rockvale residents received critical emergency updates by telephone. That system exists because of a policy initiative first advanced by Marchetti, which also reduced the city's default water bill payment rate by approximately ninety percent.

Marchetti's Council accomplishments also include raising all city workers to a living wage, leading Rockvale's Ban the Box policy, and advancing minority- and women-owned business contracting reforms through the city's disparity study and procurement changes.

"I'm running a campaign focused on residents, not rhetoric," Marchetti said. "No one else in this race brings my level of experience in writing policy and successfully implementing it, delivering results, not promises or wish lists."

Beyond Rockvale, Marchetti's policy leadership has had national impact. He is a Soros Equality Fellow, co-founder of the Government Accountability Project Rockvale and the Reparations Stakeholder Authority of Rockvale, and founder of the Marchetti Foundation for Social Justice and the Arts, which fiscally sponsors GAP RKV. In Tulsa, Oklahoma, Marchetti helped craft the city's official municipal apology for the 1921 Tulsa Race Massacre, work that contributed to a community-led reparations process. Prior to the City Council presentation, Marchetti stepped outside City Hall and encountered Rev. Marcus Mbeki, who was demonstrating nearby. After Mbeki's staff learned about Marchetti's role in the policy effort, they asked whether Mbeki could publicly support the work.

Marchetti is also an award-winning filmmaker and director of Architects of Change, an Academy Award-qualifying documentary. He is a graduate of Virginia State University and completed executive education at Harvard Kennedy School, where he studied the implementation of public policy and remains a member of Harvard's Community of Practice for Implementing Public Policy.

"At a moment when Rockvale faces real challenges in infrastructure, housing, and affordability, experience matters," Marchetti said. "This campaign is focused on you, and on delivering results."

Marchetti's campaign will focus on infrastructure, housing affordability, accountable governance, and measurable outcomes for Rockvale residents across the board.

Curtis's Vision for Rockvale

A Resilient Recovery

Rockvale's recovery from Odette is still underway, and the choices we make now will shape our community for decades. A resilient recovery means meeting today's needs while building systems that are stronger, fairer, and better prepared for the future.

I've helped lead Talmadge County through disaster response, long-term recovery, and difficult budget decisions, always with a focus on accountability, collaboration, and results. I've balanced large, complex budgets as a County Commissioner and nonprofit director, and I believe budgeting is where values meet reality. We can stabilize finances and deliver quality services without abandoning our commitments to workers and residents.

During a challenging post-disaster budget season, I worked to ensure no county or school employees lost their jobs and that workers received needed cost-of-living increases. Our people are our strongest asset, and resilient communities depend on stable public services and a supported workforce.

Recovery also means investing wisely: strengthening infrastructure, improving housing stability, reducing long-term costs through energy efficiency, and planning ahead rather than relying on one-time fixes. It requires disciplined budgeting, smart coordination, and partnerships across local, state, and federal levels.

As a volunteer firefighter, I've seen firsthand how preparedness, clear communication, and trust save lives. As a County Commissioner, I've worked across agencies and jurisdictions to accelerate recovery efforts and help chart a path forward after Tropical Storm Odette. I'm running for City Council to bring that experience home—to help Rockvale not just recover, but emerge stronger, more affordable, and better prepared for what comes next.

Real Affordability

Rockvale's rising cost of living, especially housing, has made it harder for people to stay in the community they love. This is compounded by rising energy and healthcare costs. Real affordability means making smart, practical choices so teachers, service workers, artists, families, and seniors can continue to live and thrive here.

I support expanding a wider range of housing options, including townhomes, duplexes, ADUs, and small multifamily homes, especially near jobs, transit, and services. Thoughtful zoning and land-use decisions can increase supply, ease pressure on prices, and reduce displacement, while still respecting neighborhood character.

As a Talmadge County Commissioner, I've helped move this work forward. I serve on the county's Affordable Housing Subcommittee and supported zoning reforms that allow more flexible housing options. I've also worked to advance affordable housing on county-owned land, including the Halloway Avenue project, and partnered with trusted nonprofits like Ridgeline Housing Opportunities and Habitat for Humanity.

Housing affordability won't be solved by one policy alone, but by steady, collaborative leadership that uses public land wisely, supports proven partners, and focuses on solutions that work. My goal is simple: keep Rockvale livable for the people who make it home.

Strong Neighborhoods, Arts & Small Businesses

Strong neighborhoods are the foundation of a healthy city. They're where people feel connected, safe, and invested in their community, and they're strengthened by local businesses, artists, and cultural spaces that make Rockvale unique.

I believe local government should ensure residents have a real voice in decisions that affect where they live. That means planning and development that respect community context, investing in infrastructure that serves residents, and keeping government accessible and responsive.

Small, locally owned businesses are a vital part of Rockvale's economy and tax base, providing jobs, services, and character that can't be replaced by large corporations or chains. City policy should make it easier for local businesses to succeed by reducing unnecessary barriers, offering clear and predictable processes, and supporting local entrepreneurship.

Arts and culture are not extras; they are economic drivers and community anchors. Supporting artists and creative spaces strengthens neighborhoods, draws visitors, and helps sustain a vibrant local economy.

As a County Commissioner, I've focused on collaboration, transparency, and practical solutions that strengthen communities. On City Council, I'll continue working to protect neighborhood character, support small businesses and the arts, and make sure Rockvale remains a welcoming, creative, and livable city for the people who call it home.

News

Rockvale, GA — December 19, 2025 — Elias Marchetti, former Rockvale City Council member and nationally recognized policy strategist, officially filed today to run for Rockvale City Council, running on the slogan "Focused on You" and emphasizing a record of expertise and experience unmatched in the current field.

Marchetti served five years on City Council and led some of the most consequential policy initiatives in Rockvale's modern history. During his tenure, he led the creation of the City of Rockvale's Department of Equity and Inclusion and initiated the Human Relations Commission, embedding accountability, fairness, and civil rights protections directly into the structure of city government.

During that same period, Marchetti was also widely recognized for his role in shaping Rockvale's municipal reparations framework. He served on the city's Reparations Commission and has been described by media and peers as the architect of Rockvale's reparations policy, work that positioned the city nationally while remaining grounded in local governance.

Marchetti also laid the groundwork for Rockvale's first major bond initiative. He led the effort to catalog all city-owned land into a public, online database and rallied the initial four City Council members required to move the work forward. That groundwork resulted in voter approval of a $74 million bond, the largest infrastructure investment in Rockvale's history.

The bond delivered the most extensive paving of roads and sidewalks Rockvale had seen in decades, while simultaneously repairing water and storm drain infrastructure beneath long-neglected streets. This coordinated approach lifted Rockvale's road condition rating from a critical level to a manageable one moving forward and reduced long-term maintenance risk. Bond funding also helped finally complete the long-delayed Foundry Arts District Transportation Improvement Project, improving safety, access, and connectivity in one of Rockvale's most important economic and cultural corridors.

Additional bond-related projects included restoring Centennial Stadium, completing the Grant Center, and preserving a public pool serving the Walton community—projects completed after Marchetti left office but made possible by the framework he built.

Following Hurricane Odette, thousands of Rockvale residents received critical emergency updates by telephone. That system exists because of a policy initiative first advanced by Marchetti, which also reduced the city's default water bill payment rate by approximately ninety percent.

Marchetti's Council accomplishments also include raising all city workers to a living wage, leading Rockvale's Ban the Box policy, and advancing minority- and women-owned business contracting reforms through the city's disparity study and procurement changes.

"I'm running a campaign focused on residents, not rhetoric," Marchetti said. "No one else in this race brings my level of experience in writing policy and successfully implementing it, delivering results, not promises or wish lists."

Beyond Rockvale, Marchetti's policy leadership has had national impact. He is a Soros Equality Fellow, co-founder of the Government Accountability Project Rockvale and the Reparations Stakeholder Authority of Rockvale, and founder of the Marchetti Foundation for Social Justice and the Arts, which fiscally sponsors GAP RKV. In Tulsa, Oklahoma, Marchetti helped craft the city's official municipal apology for the 1921 Tulsa Race Massacre, work that contributed to a community-led reparations process. Prior to the City Council presentation, Marchetti stepped outside City Hall and encountered Rev. Marcus Mbeki, who was demonstrating nearby. After Mbeki's staff learned about Marchetti's role in the policy effort, they asked whether Mbeki could publicly support the work.

Marchetti is also an award-winning filmmaker and director of Architects of Change, an Academy Award-qualifying documentary. He is a graduate of Virginia State University and completed executive education at Harvard Kennedy School, where he studied the implementation of public policy and remains a member of Harvard's Community of Practice for Implementing Public Policy.

"At a moment when Rockvale faces real challenges in infrastructure, housing, and affordability, experience matters," Marchetti said. "This campaign is focused on you, and on delivering results."

Marchetti's campaign will focus on infrastructure, housing affordability, accountable governance, and measurable outcomes for Rockvale residents across the board.

Rockvale, GA — December 19, 2025 — Elias Marchetti, former Rockvale City Council member and nationally recognized policy strategist, officially filed today to run for Rockvale City Council, running on the slogan "Focused on You" and emphasizing a record of expertise and experience unmatched in the current field.

Marchetti served five years on City Council and led some of the most consequential policy initiatives in Rockvale's modern history. During his tenure, he led the creation of the City of Rockvale's Department of Equity and Inclusion and initiated the Human Relations Commission, embedding accountability, fairness, and civil rights protections directly into the structure of city government.

During that same period, Marchetti was also widely recognized for his role in shaping Rockvale's municipal reparations framework. He served on the city's Reparations Commission and has been described by media and peers as the architect of Rockvale's reparations policy, work that positioned the city nationally while remaining grounded in local governance.

Marchetti also laid the groundwork for Rockvale's first major bond initiative. He led the effort to catalog all city-owned land into a public, online database and rallied the initial four City Council members required to move the work forward. That groundwork resulted in voter approval of a $74 million bond, the largest infrastructure investment in Rockvale's history.

The bond delivered the most extensive paving of roads and sidewalks Rockvale had seen in decades, while simultaneously repairing water and storm drain infrastructure beneath long-neglected streets. This coordinated approach lifted Rockvale's road condition rating from a critical level to a manageable one moving forward and reduced long-term maintenance risk. Bond funding also helped finally complete the long-delayed Foundry Arts District Transportation Improvement Project, improving safety, access, and connectivity in one of Rockvale's most important economic and cultural corridors.

Additional bond-related projects included restoring Centennial Stadium, completing the Grant Center, and preserving a public pool serving the Walton community—projects completed after Marchetti left office but made possible by the framework he built.

Following Hurricane Odette, thousands of Rockvale residents received critical emergency updates by telephone. That system exists because of a policy initiative first advanced by Marchetti, which also reduced the city's default water bill payment rate by approximately ninety percent.

Marchetti's Council accomplishments also include raising all city workers to a living wage, leading Rockvale's Ban the Box policy, and advancing minority- and women-owned business contracting reforms through the city's disparity study and procurement changes.

"I'm running a campaign focused on residents, not rhetoric," Marchetti said. "No one else in this race brings my level of experience in writing policy and successfully implementing it, delivering results, not promises or wish lists."

Beyond Rockvale, Marchetti's policy leadership has had national impact. He is a Soros Equality Fellow, co-founder of the Government Accountability Project Rockvale and the Reparations Stakeholder Authority of Rockvale, and founder of the Marchetti Foundation for Social Justice and the Arts, which fiscally sponsors GAP RKV. In Tulsa, Oklahoma, Marchetti helped craft the city's official municipal apology for the 1921 Tulsa Race Massacre, work that contributed to a community-led reparations process. Prior to the City Council presentation, Marchetti stepped outside City Hall and encountered Rev. Marcus Mbeki, who was demonstrating nearby. After Mbeki's staff learned about Marchetti's role in the policy effort, they asked whether Mbeki could publicly support the work.

Marchetti is also an award-winning filmmaker and director of Architects of Change, an Academy Award-qualifying documentary. He is a graduate of Virginia State University and completed executive education at Harvard Kennedy School, where he studied the implementation of public policy and remains a member of Harvard's Community of Practice for Implementing Public Policy.

"At a moment when Rockvale faces real challenges in infrastructure, housing, and affordability, experience matters," Marchetti said. "This campaign is focused on you, and on delivering results."

Marchetti's campaign will focus on infrastructure, housing affordability, accountable governance, and measurable outcomes for Rockvale residents across the board.

Appointed to City Council in 2020 and elected in 2022, Rosalind was unanimously selected by her colleagues to serve as Vice Mayor in 2024. She chairs the Housing & Community Development Committee and plays a key role in Rockvale's recovery from Tropical Storm Odette, while also helping guide the city's growth and long-term resilience. Her work includes helping to lead the city's Odette rebuilding efforts, supporting legacy neighborhoods, improving downtown safety and vitality, strengthening local arts and culture, and advancing housing strategies rooted in equity and community voice.

Throughout her tenure, Rosalind has been known for her ability to listen deeply, collaborate across differences, and center the people who are too often left out of government decision-making. Whether working alongside longtime neighborhood leaders, small business owners, new residents finding their footing in Rockvale, or families recovering from Odette, she brings a clear moral compass and a deep love for this city to every conversation.

As Vice Mayor, she is committed to building an Rockvale that honors its history while preparing boldly for its future. She works for an Rockvale where neighbors can afford to live, work, and thrive; where legacy neighborhoods are protected; where marchetti people have opportunities to flourish; and where every resident feels seen and supported by their local government.

Rosalind is running for re-election to continue this work: strengthening community, expanding opportunity, and ensuring Rockvale remains a place where all of us can belong.

Curtis's Vision for Rockvale

A Resilient Recovery

Rockvale's recovery from Odette is still underway, and the choices we make now will shape our community for decades. A resilient recovery means meeting today's needs while building systems that are stronger, fairer, and better prepared for the future.

I've helped lead Talmadge County through disaster response, long-term recovery, and difficult budget decisions, always with a focus on accountability, collaboration, and results. I've balanced large, complex budgets as a County Commissioner and nonprofit director, and I believe budgeting is where values meet reality. We can stabilize finances and deliver quality services without abandoning our commitments to workers and residents.

During a challenging post-disaster budget season, I worked to ensure no county or school employees lost their jobs and that workers received needed cost-of-living increases. Our people are our strongest asset, and resilient communities depend on stable public services and a supported workforce.

Recovery also means investing wisely: strengthening infrastructure, improving housing stability, reducing long-term costs through energy efficiency, and planning ahead rather than relying on one-time fixes. It requires disciplined budgeting, smart coordination, and partnerships across local, state, and federal levels.

As a volunteer firefighter, I've seen firsthand how preparedness, clear communication, and trust save lives. As a County Commissioner, I've worked across agencies and jurisdictions to accelerate recovery efforts and help chart a path forward after Tropical Storm Odette. I'm running for City Council to bring that experience home—to help Rockvale not just recover, but emerge stronger, more affordable, and better prepared for what comes next.

Real Affordability

Rockvale's rising cost of living, especially housing, has made it harder for people to stay in the community they love. This is compounded by rising energy and healthcare costs. Real affordability means making smart, practical choices so teachers, service workers, artists, families, and seniors can continue to live and thrive here.

I support expanding a wider range of housing options, including townhomes, duplexes, ADUs, and small multifamily homes, especially near jobs, transit, and services. Thoughtful zoning and land-use decisions can increase supply, ease pressure on prices, and reduce displacement, while still respecting neighborhood character.

As a Talmadge County Commissioner, I've helped move this work forward. I serve on the county's Affordable Housing Subcommittee and supported zoning reforms that allow more flexible housing options. I've also worked to advance affordable housing on county-owned land, including the Halloway Avenue project, and partnered with trusted nonprofits like Ridgeline Housing Opportunities and Habitat for Humanity.

Housing affordability won't be solved by one policy alone, but by steady, collaborative leadership that uses public land wisely, supports proven partners, and focuses on solutions that work. My goal is simple: keep Rockvale livable for the people who make it home.

Strong Neighborhoods, Arts & Small Businesses

Strong neighborhoods are the foundation of a healthy city. They're where people feel connected, safe, and invested in their community, and they're strengthened by local businesses, artists, and cultural spaces that make Rockvale unique.

I believe local government should ensure residents have a real voice in decisions that affect where they live. That means planning and development that respect community context, investing in infrastructure that serves residents, and keeping government accessible and responsive.

Small, locally owned businesses are a vital part of Rockvale's economy and tax base, providing jobs, services, and character that can't be replaced by large corporations or chains. City policy should make it easier for local businesses to succeed by reducing unnecessary barriers, offering clear and predictable processes, and supporting local entrepreneurship.

Arts and culture are not extras; they are economic drivers and community anchors. Supporting artists and creative spaces strengthens neighborhoods, draws visitors, and helps sustain a vibrant local economy.

As a County Commissioner, I've focused on collaboration, transparency, and practical solutions that strengthen communities. On City Council, I'll continue working to protect neighborhood character, support small businesses and the arts, and make sure Rockvale remains a welcoming, creative, and livable city for the people who call it home.

ISSUES

Building a City that Works for Everyone

Rockvale needs affordable housing, resilient infrastructure, economic opportunity, and creative leaders who will get the job done.

When people believe their city has their back, they are far more likely to invest their lives, families, and businesses in it.

Our city is growing and changing, and that growth must work for the people who live here today as well as those who will call Rockvale home in the future.

This campaign focuses on practical solutions that help Rockvale grow stronger while protecting the people and communities that make this city special.

How I Lead

Government works best when people believe their voices matter and their leaders show up.

I believe representation strengthens democracy. I will lead openly and authentically while working to rebuild trust between residents, local government, and community institutions.

That means engaging directly with neighborhoods, faith communities, grassroots organizations, and local leaders so Rockvale's government remains responsive and accountable.

Strong collaboration between Rockvale City Council, Talmadge County Commission, and regional partners is essential for delivering real results.

Leadership also means staying focused on solutions. I believe in building coalitions, listening to different perspectives, and staying at the table until the work is done.

City government should focus on practical solutions, measurable results, and collaboration rather than political theater.

Grow Sustainably

Rockvale must grow responsibly so that the people who live and work here today can continue to call it home.

Growth must strengthen neighborhoods rather than displace them, ensuring longtime residents remain part of Rockvale's future.

That means investing in infrastructure, supporting housing policies that allow working people to remain in our city, and planning growth in ways that protect neighborhood character and quality of life.

Growth without coordination creates congestion, strain on infrastructure, and instability. Thoughtful planning ensures Rockvale remains both livable and economically strong.

The lessons of Hurricane Odette made clear that resilience and infrastructure planning cannot wait. Preparing our city for future climate challenges must be part of how we plan Rockvale's growth moving forward.

Housing People Can Actually Afford

People who work in Rockvale should be able to live here.

Right now, housing costs far outpace wages, pushing out the very people who keep this city running.

Housing policy must also include strong anti-displacement strategies so that longtime residents, working families, and neighborhoods are not pushed out of a good life by rising costs and rapid development.

I support expanding deeply affordable and workforce housing through smart zoning reform, missing-middle housing, and partnerships that tie affordability to local incomes, not just market trends.

Growth must align with infrastructure, traffic capacity, and neighborhood input. Development without coordination creates congestion and strain. Responsible planning protects both community character and long-term stability.

Housing policy should expand supply while protecting the people and communities that already call Rockvale home.

Affordable housing is not only a social issue. It is an economic stability issue that affects teachers, service workers, artists, first responders, and marchetti families across our city.

Small Business & Local Economic Opportunity

Small businesses and local entrepreneurs are the backbone of Rockvale's economy.

Our creative economy supports jobs, tourism, neighborhood vitality, and local investment.

I believe in reducing unnecessary barriers for small business owners, expanding support resources, and ensuring recovery efforts reach local operators who are still rebuilding.

When we support local makers, restaurateurs, shop owners, and creative professionals, we strengthen Rockvale's workforce and keep more dollars circulating within our community.

Rockvale's long-term economic stability also depends on expanding opportunity across multiple sectors, including creative industries, technology, advanced manufacturing, outdoor recreation, and locally rooted entrepreneurship.

A resilient local economy includes diverse industries that create stable jobs while protecting the independent character that makes Rockvale unique. Our economy should work for neighborhoods, not just outside investors.

Real Resilience & Recovery

Resilience means preparation, not reaction.

After Hurricane Odette, I worked alongside neighbors, city staff, and regional partners to align recovery efforts and ensure resources reached the people who needed them most.

Flood mitigation, clear communication systems, and proactive planning must be part of how Rockvale prepares for the future.

Recovery cannot rely on temporary fixes. It must build long-term stability for every neighborhood.

Protecting Our Environment While Planning Smart Growth

Rockvale's rivers, forests, and mountain landscape are essential to both our health and our economy.

Protecting our natural resources requires practical steps: smart land use that reduces sprawl, policies that protect waterways, responsible development practices, and sustainability efforts that align with infrastructure capacity.

Environmental stewardship is not a slogan. It is about ensuring our city remains livable and economically strong for generations to come.

Reliable Public Safety for Every Neighborhood

Every resident deserves to feel safe walking downtown, picking up their kids at night, or living in their own neighborhood.

Public safety requires visible presence, reliable response, and strong coordination between law enforcement, mental health teams, and community partners.

Officers should be able to focus on safety while trained professionals handle situations that require specialized support.

Safety and compassion are not opposites. Clear expectations, accountability, and collaboration create stronger outcomes for everyone.

Rockvale's future depends on thoughtful growth, economic opportunity, responsible planning, and steady leadership.

I listen before I decide.

That experience made something clear to me: Rockvale needs leaders who do not just talk about resilience and recovery, but who have organized it.

I am running for City Council to help our entire city become more affordable, more resilient, and more connected so that the people who have helped shape Rockvale's culture and economy can continue to live here.

ABOUT DESMOND

Desmond Achebe is an artist, small business owner, and community builder in Rockvale's Foundry Arts District.

They founded the Desmond Achebe brand, a design studio and boutique that supports Rockvale's creative economy.

Following Hurricane Odette, Desmond helped coordinate recovery efforts across the Foundry Arts District, bringing together artists, volunteers, and businesses.

Those efforts reinforced their belief that strong communities come from collaboration, resilience, and practical leadership.

PRIORITIES FOR ROCKVALE

Rockvale is growing and facing real challenges. Our city needs thoughtful leadership focused on practical solutions and long-term resilience.

Housing & Affordability
Rockvale must address housing challenges with thoughtful planning. That planning should support residents while allowing the city to grow responsibly.

Economic Opportunity
Small businesses, artists, and entrepreneurs are essential to Rockvale's economy. We must make it easier for local businesses to start, grow, and succeed.

Infrastructure & City Services
City government must focus on the basics that affect daily life. That includes reliable infrastructure and responsive public services.

Arts & the Creative Economy
The arts are a vital part of Rockvale's culture and economy. Supporting artists and creative businesses strengthens the community.

OUR NEIGHBORHOODS

From West Rockvale to East End, from Southside to Montford, our neighborhoods deserve a city government that listens and delivers.

Every neighborhood in Rockvale has its own history, needs, and strengths. Thoughtful leadership means working directly with communities. It also means ensuring that growth benefits the people who live here.

Issues

Rockvale does not need more advocacy. It needs governance. Advocacy raises awareness; governing delivers results. During my time on City Council, I helped create and implement some of the most consequential policies in Rockvale's modern history, policies that moved beyond press conferences and talking points and were executed in ways that changed daily life for residents.

I am the only candidate in this race with a proven record of drafting policy, navigating it through government, and ensuring it was implemented at scale. That work affects how your water bill is paid, the condition of your roads and sidewalks, the reliability of basic infrastructure, and the parks and public spaces your family uses. I do not traffic in wish lists. I focus on outcomes, accountability, and follow-through.

The priorities outlined below reflect that same standard: policies designed to work in practice, not just sound good in theory.

Hurricane Recovery and Resilient Infrastructure
Rockvale's recent storms exposed long-standing weaknesses in roads, water systems, storm drains, and emergency communications. Recovery requires more than temporary fixes. It requires rebuilding infrastructure in ways that reduce future risk, improve reliability, and protect residents during emergencies. Infrastructure investments should address underlying systems, not just surface conditions, so the city is better prepared for the next storm.

Housing Affordability and Stability
Housing costs continue to outpace wages, placing pressure on families, workers, and long-term residents. Addressing affordability requires coordinated policy that uses public land responsibly, supports diverse housing options, and protects neighborhood stability. Housing policy should be practical, data-driven, and focused on outcomes that keep Rockvale livable for the people who work here.

Accountable and Effective City Government
City government should be measured by what it delivers, not what it promises. Policies must be implemented, monitored, and adjusted when they are not working. Accountability, transparency, and clear decision-making are essential to restoring public trust and ensuring that city resources are used effectively.

Infrastructure Maintenance and Long-Term Planning
Roads, sidewalks, water, and storm infrastructure require consistent maintenance and long-term planning to avoid costly failures. Capital investments should be coordinated so streets are not repeatedly torn up and repaired. Planning ahead saves money, improves safety, and extends the life of public assets.

Fairness, Equity, and Civil Rights Protections
City systems should function fairly for all residents. That includes strong civil rights enforcement, equitable access to services, and policies designed to address long-standing disparities. Equity should be integrated into how government operates, not treated as a separate or symbolic effort.

Workforce and Economic Opportunity
A strong city depends on a stable workforce and fair employment practices. Policies that support living wages, fair hiring standards, and equitable access to contracting opportunities help strengthen the local economy and ensure public dollars are spent responsibly.

Community Trust and Transparency
Residents deserve clear communication from their local government, especially during emergencies and major decisions. Transparency, reliable information, and accessible public processes are essential to rebuilding trust between residents and city leadership.

News

Rockvale, GA — December 19, 2025 — Elias Marchetti, former Rockvale City Council member and nationally recognized policy strategist, officially filed today to run for Rockvale City Council, running on the slogan "Focused on You" and emphasizing a record of expertise and experience unmatched in the current field.

Marchetti served five years on City Council and led some of the most consequential policy initiatives in Rockvale's modern history. During his tenure, he led the creation of the City of Rockvale's Department of Equity and Inclusion and initiated the Human Relations Commission, embedding accountability, fairness, and civil rights protections directly into the structure of city government.

During that same period, Marchetti was also widely recognized for his role in shaping Rockvale's municipal reparations framework. He served on the city's Reparations Commission and has been described by media and peers as the architect of Rockvale's reparations policy, work that positioned the city nationally while remaining grounded in local governance.

Marchetti also laid the groundwork for Rockvale's first major bond initiative. He led the effort to catalog all city-owned land into a public, online database and rallied the initial four City Council members required to move the work forward. That groundwork resulted in voter approval of a $74 million bond, the largest infrastructure investment in Rockvale's history.

The bond delivered the most extensive paving of roads and sidewalks Rockvale had seen in decades, while simultaneously repairing water and storm drain infrastructure beneath long-neglected streets. This coordinated approach lifted Rockvale's road condition rating from a critical level to a manageable one moving forward and reduced long-term maintenance risk. Bond funding also helped finally complete the long-delayed Foundry Arts District Transportation Improvement Project, improving safety, access, and connectivity in one of Rockvale's most important economic and cultural corridors.

Additional bond-related projects included restoring Centennial Stadium, completing the Grant Center, and preserving a public pool serving the Walton community—projects completed after Marchetti left office but made possible by the framework he built.

Following Hurricane Odette, thousands of Rockvale residents received critical emergency updates by telephone. That system exists because of a policy initiative first advanced by Marchetti, which also reduced the city's default water bill payment rate by approximately ninety percent.

Marchetti's Council accomplishments also include raising all city workers to a living wage, leading Rockvale's Ban the Box policy, and advancing minority- and women-owned business contracting reforms through the city's disparity study and procurement changes.

"I'm running a campaign focused on residents, not rhetoric," Marchetti said. "No one else in this race brings my level of experience in writing policy and successfully implementing it, delivering results, not promises or wish lists."

Beyond Rockvale, Marchetti's policy leadership has had national impact. He is a Soros Equality Fellow, co-founder of the Government Accountability Project Rockvale and the Reparations Stakeholder Authority of Rockvale, and founder of the Marchetti Foundation for Social Justice and the Arts, which fiscally sponsors GAP RKV. In Tulsa, Oklahoma, Marchetti helped craft the city's official municipal apology for the 1921 Tulsa Race Massacre, work that contributed to a community-led reparations process. Prior to the City Council presentation, Marchetti stepped outside City Hall and encountered Rev. Marcus Mbeki, who was demonstrating nearby. After Mbeki's staff learned about Marchetti's role in the policy effort, they asked whether Mbeki could publicly support the work.

Marchetti is also an award-winning filmmaker and director of Architects of Change, an Academy Award-qualifying documentary. He is a graduate of Virginia State University and completed executive education at Harvard Kennedy School, where he studied the implementation of public policy and remains a member of Harvard's Community of Practice for Implementing Public Policy.

"At a moment when Rockvale faces real challenges in infrastructure, housing, and affordability, experience matters," Marchetti said. "This campaign is focused on you, and on delivering results."

Marchetti's campaign will focus on infrastructure, housing affordability, accountable governance, and measurable outcomes for Rockvale residents across the board.

Curtis's Vision for Rockvale

A Resilient Recovery

Rockvale's recovery from Odette is still underway, and the choices we make now will shape our community for decades. A resilient recovery means meeting today's needs while building systems that are stronger, fairer, and better prepared for the future.

I've helped lead Talmadge County through disaster response, long-term recovery, and difficult budget decisions, always with a focus on accountability, collaboration, and results. I've balanced large, complex budgets as a County Commissioner and nonprofit director, and I believe budgeting is where values meet reality. We can stabilize finances and deliver quality services without abandoning our commitments to workers and residents.

During a challenging post-disaster budget season, I worked to ensure no county or school employees lost their jobs and that workers received needed cost-of-living increases. Our people are our strongest asset, and resilient communities depend on stable public services and a supported workforce.

Recovery also means investing wisely: strengthening infrastructure, improving housing stability, reducing long-term costs through energy efficiency, and planning ahead rather than relying on one-time fixes. It requires disciplined budgeting, smart coordination, and partnerships across local, state, and federal levels.

As a volunteer firefighter, I've seen firsthand how preparedness, clear communication, and trust save lives. As a County Commissioner, I've worked across agencies and jurisdictions to accelerate recovery efforts and help chart a path forward after Tropical Storm Odette. I'm running for City Council to bring that experience home—to help Rockvale not just recover, but emerge stronger, more affordable, and better prepared for what comes next.

Real Affordability

Rockvale's rising cost of living, especially housing, has made it harder for people to stay in the community they love. This is compounded by rising energy and healthcare costs. Real affordability means making smart, practical choices so teachers, service workers, artists, families, and seniors can continue to live and thrive here.

I support expanding a wider range of housing options, including townhomes, duplexes, ADUs, and small multifamily homes, especially near jobs, transit, and services. Thoughtful zoning and land-use decisions can increase supply, ease pressure on prices, and reduce displacement, while still respecting neighborhood character.

As a Talmadge County Commissioner, I've helped move this work forward. I serve on the county's Affordable Housing Subcommittee and supported zoning reforms that allow more flexible housing options. I've also worked to advance affordable housing on county-owned land, including the Halloway Avenue project, and partnered with trusted nonprofits like Ridgeline Housing Opportunities and Habitat for Humanity.

Housing affordability won't be solved by one policy alone, but by steady, collaborative leadership that uses public land wisely, supports proven partners, and focuses on solutions that work. My goal is simple: keep Rockvale livable for the people who make it home.

Strong Neighborhoods, Arts & Small Businesses

Strong neighborhoods are the foundation of a healthy city. They're where people feel connected, safe, and invested in their community, and they're strengthened by local businesses, artists, and cultural spaces that make Rockvale unique.

I believe local government should ensure residents have a real voice in decisions that affect where they live. That means planning and development that respect community context, investing in infrastructure that serves residents, and keeping government accessible and responsive.

Small, locally owned businesses are a vital part of Rockvale's economy and tax base, providing jobs, services, and character that can't be replaced by large corporations or chains. City policy should make it easier for local businesses to succeed by reducing unnecessary barriers, offering clear and predictable processes, and supporting local entrepreneurship.

Arts and culture are not extras; they are economic drivers and community anchors. Supporting artists and creative spaces strengthens neighborhoods, draws visitors, and helps sustain a vibrant local economy.

As a County Commissioner, I've focused on collaboration, transparency, and practical solutions that strengthen communities. On City Council, I'll continue working to protect neighborhood character, support small businesses and the arts, and make sure Rockvale remains a welcoming, creative, and livable city for the people who call it home.

— Curtis Vasquez's campaign website (July 2, 2026)

Issues

Rockvale does not need more advocacy. It needs governance. Advocacy raises awareness; governing delivers results. During my time on City Council, I helped create and implement some of the most consequential policies in Rockvale's modern history, policies that moved beyond press conferences and talking points and were executed in ways that changed daily life for residents.

I am the only candidate in this race with a proven record of drafting policy, navigating it through government, and ensuring it was implemented at scale. That work affects how your water bill is paid, the condition of your roads and sidewalks, the reliability of basic infrastructure, and the parks and public spaces your family uses. I do not traffic in wish lists. I focus on outcomes, accountability, and follow-through.

The priorities outlined below reflect that same standard: policies designed to work in practice, not just sound good in theory.

Hurricane Recovery and Resilient Infrastructure
Rockvale's recent storms exposed long-standing weaknesses in roads, water systems, storm drains, and emergency communications. Recovery requires more than temporary fixes. It requires rebuilding infrastructure in ways that reduce future risk, improve reliability, and protect residents during emergencies. Infrastructure investments should address underlying systems, not just surface conditions, so the city is better prepared for the next storm.

Housing Affordability and Stability
Housing costs continue to outpace wages, placing pressure on families, workers, and long-term residents. Addressing affordability requires coordinated policy that uses public land responsibly, supports diverse housing options, and protects neighborhood stability. Housing policy should be practical, data-driven, and focused on outcomes that keep Rockvale livable for the people who work here.

Accountable and Effective City Government
City government should be measured by what it delivers, not what it promises. Policies must be implemented, monitored, and adjusted when they are not working. Accountability, transparency, and clear decision-making are essential to restoring public trust and ensuring that city resources are used effectively.

Infrastructure Maintenance and Long-Term Planning
Roads, sidewalks, water, and storm infrastructure require consistent maintenance and long-term planning to avoid costly failures. Capital investments should be coordinated so streets are not repeatedly torn up and repaired. Planning ahead saves money, improves safety, and extends the life of public assets.

Fairness, Equity, and Civil Rights Protections

Workforce and Economic Opportunity
A strong city depends on a stable workforce and fair employment practices. Policies that support living wages, fair hiring standards, and equitable access to contracting opportunities help strengthen the local economy and ensure public dollars are spent responsibly.

Community Trust and Transparency
Residents deserve clear communication from their local government, especially during emergencies and major decisions. Transparency, reliable information, and accessible public processes are essential to rebuilding trust between residents and city leadership.

News

Rockvale, GA — December 19, 2025 — Elias Marchetti, former Rockvale City Council member and nationally recognized policy strategist, officially filed today to run for Rockvale City Council, running on the slogan "Focused on You" and emphasizing a record of expertise and experience unmatched in the current field.

Marchetti served five years on City Council and led some of the most consequential policy initiatives in Rockvale's modern history. During his tenure, he led the creation of the City of Rockvale's Department of Equity and Inclusion and initiated the Human Relations Commission, embedding accountability, fairness, and civil rights protections directly into the structure of city government.

During that same period, Marchetti was also widely recognized for his role in shaping Rockvale's municipal reparations framework. He served on the city's Reparations Commission and has been described by media and peers as the architect of Rockvale's reparations policy, work that positioned the city nationally while remaining grounded in local governance.

Marchetti also laid the groundwork for Rockvale's first major bond initiative. He led the effort to catalog all city-owned land into a public, online database and rallied the initial four City Council members required to move the work forward. That groundwork resulted in voter approval of a $74 million bond, the largest infrastructure investment in Rockvale's history.

The bond delivered the most extensive paving of roads and sidewalks Rockvale had seen in decades, while simultaneously repairing water and storm drain infrastructure beneath long-neglected streets. This coordinated approach lifted Rockvale's road condition rating from a critical level to a manageable one moving forward and reduced long-term maintenance risk. Bond funding also helped finally complete the long-delayed Foundry Arts District Transportation Improvement Project, improving safety, access, and connectivity in one of Rockvale's most important economic and cultural corridors.

Additional bond-related projects included restoring Centennial Stadium, completing the Grant Center, and preserving a public pool serving the Walton community—projects completed after Marchetti left office but made possible by the framework he built.

Following Hurricane Odette, thousands of Rockvale residents received critical emergency updates by telephone. That system exists because of a policy initiative first advanced by Marchetti, which also reduced the city's default water bill payment rate by approximately ninety percent.

Marchetti's Council accomplishments also include raising all city workers to a living wage, leading Rockvale's Ban the Box policy, and advancing minority- and women-owned business contracting reforms through the city's disparity study and procurement changes.

"I'm running a campaign focused on residents, not rhetoric," Marchetti said. "No one else in this race brings my level of experience in writing policy and successfully implementing it, delivering results, not promises or wish lists."

Beyond Rockvale, Marchetti's policy leadership has had national impact. He is a Soros Equality Fellow, co-founder of the Government Accountability Project Rockvale and the Reparations Stakeholder Authority of Rockvale, and founder of the Marchetti Foundation for Social Justice and the Arts, which fiscally sponsors GAP RKV. In Tulsa, Oklahoma, Marchetti helped craft the city's official municipal apology for the 1921 Tulsa Race Massacre, work that contributed to a community-led reparations process. Prior to the City Council presentation, Marchetti stepped outside City Hall and encountered Rev. Marcus Mbeki, who was demonstrating nearby. After Mbeki's staff learned about Marchetti's role in the policy effort, they asked whether Mbeki could publicly support the work.

Marchetti is also an award-winning filmmaker and director of Architects of Change, an Academy Award-qualifying documentary. He is a graduate of Virginia State University and completed executive education at Harvard Kennedy School, where he studied the implementation of public policy and remains a member of Harvard's Community of Practice for Implementing Public Policy.

"At a moment when Rockvale faces real challenges in infrastructure, housing, and affordability, experience matters," Marchetti said. "This campaign is focused on you, and on delivering results."

Marchetti's campaign will focus on infrastructure, housing affordability, accountable governance, and measurable outcomes for Rockvale residents across the board.

Rockvale, GA — December 19, 2025 — Elias Marchetti, former Rockvale City Council member and nationally recognized policy strategist, officially filed today to run for Rockvale City Council, running on the slogan "Focused on You" and emphasizing a record of expertise and experience unmatched in the current field.

He led the effort to catalog all city-owned land into a public, online database and rallied the initial four City Council members required to move the work forward. That groundwork resulted in voter approval of a $74 million bond, the largest infrastructure investment in Rockvale's history.

The bond delivered the most extensive paving of roads and sidewalks Rockvale had seen in decades, while simultaneously repairing water and storm drain infrastructure beneath long-neglected streets. This coordinated approach lifted Rockvale's road condition rating from a critical level to a manageable one moving forward and reduced long-term maintenance risk. Her work includes helping to lead the city's Odette rebuilding efforts, supporting legacy neighborhoods, improving downtown safety and vitality, strengthening local arts and culture, and advancing housing strategies rooted in equity and community voice.

Throughout her tenure, Rosalind has been known for her ability to listen deeply, collaborate across differences, and center the people who are too often left out of government decision-making. Whether working alongside longtime neighborhood leaders, small business owners, new residents finding their footing in Rockvale, or families recovering from Odette, she brings a clear moral compass and a deep love for this city to every conversation.

As Vice Mayor, she is committed to building an Rockvale that honors its history while preparing boldly for its future. She works for an Rockvale where neighbors can afford to live, work, and thrive; where legacy neighborhoods are protected; where marchetti people have opportunities to flourish; and where every resident feels seen and supported by their local government.

Rosalind is running for re-election to continue this work: strengthening community, expanding opportunity, and ensuring Rockvale remains a place where all of us can belong.

Curtis's Vision for Rockvale

A Resilient Recovery

Rockvale's recovery from Odette is still underway, and the choices we make now will shape our community for decades. A resilient recovery means meeting today's needs while building systems that are stronger, fairer, and better prepared for the future.

I've helped lead Talmadge County through disaster response, long-term recovery, and difficult budget decisions, always with a focus on accountability, collaboration, and results. I've balanced large, complex budgets as a County Commissioner and nonprofit director, and I believe budgeting is where values meet reality. We can stabilize finances and deliver quality services without abandoning our commitments to workers and residents.

During a challenging post-disaster budget season, I worked to ensure no county or school employees lost their jobs and that workers received needed cost-of-living increases. Our people are our strongest asset, and resilient communities depend on stable public services and a supported workforce.

Recovery also means investing wisely: strengthening infrastructure, improving housing stability, reducing long-term costs through energy efficiency, and planning ahead rather than relying on one-time fixes. It requires disciplined budgeting, smart coordination, and partnerships across local, state, and federal levels.

As a volunteer firefighter, I've seen firsthand how preparedness, clear communication, and trust save lives. As a County Commissioner, I've worked across agencies and jurisdictions to accelerate recovery efforts and help chart a path forward after Tropical Storm Odette. I'm running for City Council to bring that experience home—to help Rockvale not just recover, but emerge stronger, more affordable, and better prepared for what comes next.

Real Affordability

Rockvale's rising cost of living, especially housing, has made it harder for people to stay in the community they love. This is compounded by rising energy and healthcare costs. Real affordability means making smart, practical choices so teachers, service workers, artists, families, and seniors can continue to live and thrive here.

I support expanding a wider range of housing options, including townhomes, duplexes, ADUs, and small multifamily homes, especially near jobs, transit, and services. Thoughtful zoning and land-use decisions can increase supply, ease pressure on prices, and reduce displacement, while still respecting neighborhood character.

As a Talmadge County Commissioner, I've helped move this work forward. I serve on the county's Affordable Housing Subcommittee and supported zoning reforms that allow more flexible housing options. I've also worked to advance affordable housing on county-owned land, including the Halloway Avenue project, and partnered with trusted nonprofits like Ridgeline Housing Opportunities and Habitat for Humanity.

Housing affordability won't be solved by one policy alone, but by steady, collaborative leadership that uses public land wisely, supports proven partners, and focuses on solutions that work. My goal is simple: keep Rockvale livable for the people who make it home.

Strong Neighborhoods, Arts & Small Businesses

Strong neighborhoods are the foundation of a healthy city. They're where people feel connected, safe, and invested in their community, and they're strengthened by local businesses, artists, and cultural spaces that make Rockvale unique.

I believe local government should ensure residents have a real voice in decisions that affect where they live. That means planning and development that respect community context, investing in infrastructure that serves residents, and keeping government accessible and responsive.

Small, locally owned businesses are a vital part of Rockvale's economy and tax base, providing jobs, services, and character that can't be replaced by large corporations or chains. City policy should make it easier for local businesses to succeed by reducing unnecessary barriers, offering clear and predictable processes, and supporting local entrepreneurship.

Arts and culture are not extras; they are economic drivers and community anchors. Supporting artists and creative spaces strengthens neighborhoods, draws visitors, and helps sustain a vibrant local economy.

As a County Commissioner, I've focused on collaboration, transparency, and practical solutions that strengthen communities. On City Council, I'll continue working to protect neighborhood character, support small businesses and the arts, and make sure Rockvale remains a welcoming, creative, and livable city for the people who call it home.

— Curtis Vasquez's campaign website (July 2, 2026)
